source_text: Praedico omnem in eo sanctitatem beneficio animi, non carnis stetisse praeiudicio. Sic enim et natura tam conditione eius quam susceptione de fenditur, et vita hominum virtutum illius imitatione dirigitur. De his duobus non potest alterum sine alterius veritate laudari; tantum aderit dignitatis operi sacro, quantum humani corporis adfuerit veritati; et tantum aderit defensioni carnis, quantum sanctitas conversationis exegerit. Atque e regione, vituperatio unius utrique participat; quoniam tantum de virtutibus eius, quantum de artubus auferetur; ac si quid de substantiae solido radatur, universa morum ornamenta depereunt, atque ad tolerantis iniuriam recurrunt damna nascentis; postremo si carnis eius substantia aliqua naturalium ereptione tenuetur, universa evanescit pompa virtutum. Nihil ergo in membris Mediatoris facti ex muliere, quod naturale constat, negabo. Et vide quam diversi sint rationis termini, quam pudoris; non erubescit fides Christianorum, dicere Christum habuisse genitalia; cum tamen ea in nobis, quam honestissime possumus, occulamus.
pass_a_gloss: I proclaim that every holiness in him stood by the benefit of the mind, not by a prior judgment of the flesh. For thus both nature is defended as much by his condition as by his taking-up, and the life of humans is directed by imitation of his virtues. Of these two, one cannot be praised without the truth of the other; so much dignity will be present to the sacred work as shall have been present to the truth of the human body; and so much will be present to the defense of the flesh as the holiness of the way of life shall have demanded. And from the opposite side, the blaming of one shares in both; because so much will be taken away from his virtues as from his limbs; and if anything is scraped from the solid of the substance, all the ornaments of manners perish, and the losses of the one being born run back to the injury of the one enduring; finally if the substance of his flesh is thinned by some snatching of natural things, the whole pomp of virtues vanishes. I will therefore deny nothing in the members of the Mediator made from a woman, which stands as natural. And see how diverse the limits of reason are, and those of modesty; the faith of Christians does not blush to say that Christ had genitals; although nevertheless we hide them in us as honorably as we can.

pass_b_english: I proclaim that all his holiness rested on the benefit of his mind, not on an exemption granted to his flesh. In this way nature is defended both by his creation of it and by his assumption of it, and human life is directed by imitation of his virtues. Neither of these two things can be praised without the truth of the other. His sacred work will have as much dignity as his human body has reality; and the defense of his flesh will extend as far as the holiness of his life requires. Conversely, blame of one affects both. As much will be taken from his virtues as is taken from his limbs. If anything is scraped away from the solidity of his substance, all the adornments of his conduct perish; and losses inflicted on the one born return as an insult to the one who suffered. In short, if the substance of his flesh is reduced by removing any natural property, the entire display of virtues vanishes.

I will therefore deny nothing in the members of the Mediator, made from a woman, that is known to be natural (compare Galatians 4:4). And see how different the boundaries of reason and modesty are. The Christian faith is not ashamed to say that Christ had genitals, although we conceal them in ourselves as decently as we can.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
